If you call a person or their behavior Machiavellian, you mean they are cunningly clever, deeply manipulative, and willing to use deceit and ruthless tactics to get what they want — usually power, control, or personal gain — without any guilt or moral concern.

It is almost always used as a negative word.
Where the Idea Comes From

The word comes from a real man: Niccolò Machiavelli, an Italian political thinker who lived in the 1400s–1500s. He wrote a famous book called The Prince, where he advised rulers that to gain and keep power, a leader must be willing to lie, manipulate, and even be cruel when necessary. He argued that results matter more than the methods used to get them.

Over time, his name became the label for this entire way of thinking and behaving.
The Heart of the Meaning

The core idea behind "Machiavellian" is a famous principle:

"The ends justify the means."

This means: it doesn't matter how dirty, dishonest, or harmful your methods are, as long as you achieve your goal.

A Machiavellian person genuinely believes — or at least operates as if — this is true.
What a Machiavellian Person Actually Looks Like

Here are the key traits, broken down clearly:

1. They are strategic and calculating.
They don't act impulsively. They plan several steps ahead, always thinking: "How does this move benefit me in the long run?"

2. They manipulate people skillfully.
They know how to push people's emotional buttons — using flattery, fear, guilt, or false sympathy — to steer others toward doing what they want. The other person often doesn't even realize they're being manipulated.

3. They wear a mask.
A Machiavellian person can appear charming, loyal, and trustworthy on the surface. They are skilled actors. Their real intentions are hidden underneath. This is what makes them dangerous — they don't look like a threat.

4. They have no loyalty — only usefulness.
They will befriend you, use you, and drop you the moment you are no longer useful to them. Relationships are tools, not bonds.

5. They lie without guilt.
Honesty is a strategy, not a value, to them. They will tell the truth when it benefits them and lie when it doesn't — and they feel no internal conflict about it.

6. They are patient.
Unlike simply selfish or aggressive people, a Machiavellian person will wait, play nice, and bide their time until the moment is right to make their move.
A Real-Life Example

Imagine a coworker, Sarah. She smiles at you every day, asks about your family, and acts like your best friend at work. But quietly, she has been taking credit for your ideas in meetings you didn't attend. She told the manager that she carried the last project, while subtly suggesting you were unhelpful. When she finally gets the promotion you both wanted, she thanks you publicly — and means none of it.

Sarah's behavior is Machiavellian. She used charm as a disguise, manipulated perceptions behind the scenes, felt no guilt about the dishonesty, and achieved her personal goal at your expense.
The Difference Between Machiavellian and Just Being Smart or Ambitious

This is an important distinction.

  • A smart, ambitious person works hard, competes fairly, and may be tough or assertive — but they operate within ethical limits.
  • A Machiavellian person has no ethical limit. Morality is simply irrelevant to them when it conflicts with their goals.

Being clever is not Machiavellian. Being cunningly manipulative and morally unrestrained in pursuit of power is.
It Can Describe People, Plans, and Behaviors

The word isn't only used for people. It can describe:

  • A Machiavellian scheme — a complex, devious plan designed to deceive others
  • Machiavellian politics — political maneuvering that uses manipulation and deception
  • Machiavellian tactics — specific moves or actions that are underhanded and calculated
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "His Machiavellian approach to climbing the corporate ladder left a trail of betrayed colleagues."
  • "She hatched a Machiavellian plan to turn her two rivals against each other so she could win unopposed."
  • "The villain in the story was truly Machiavellian — always smiling, always scheming."
The Tone: Always a Warning Sign

When someone is called Machiavellian, it is a serious accusation. It doesn't just mean they were rude, selfish, or even dishonest once. It means they are systemically and deliberately manipulative in a way that is calculated and cold. It suggests a personality — not just a bad day or a single bad choice.

In psychology, Machiavellianism is actually recognized as one of the "Dark Triad" personality traits (along with narcissism and psychopathy), used to describe people who are especially prone to manipulation and lack of empathy.
The One-Sentence Summary

A Machiavellian person is a calculating, charming, and deeply deceptive individual who will say anything, use anyone, and cross any moral line to gain power or achieve their goals — all while hiding their true nature behind a convincing, friendly face.
